\chapter{Counting To Five, And The One New Sign}
\label{ch:mw-count-five}
\hlchaptermodality{32}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hear, say, read, and write the numbers one to five, after learning only \mw{ए}.}

One new letter is isolated, then five numbers are built on signs the hand already had, and all five pass separately in listening, speaking, reading, and writing.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[e]{\mw{ए} — the mark, standing on its own}

\label{lesson:MW-W32-e}



\begin{quote}
Write vegetables, then final, then \textbf{\mw{पाछे} \mw{मिलसू}}. Point at the stroke above the head-line in each one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the standing vowel}
Since chapter 7 the hand has made \textbf{\mw{े}} — a short stroke hung above the head-line, riding on a consonant. It never stands by itself, because a mark is what a vowel looks like when a consonant is already carrying it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{ए}} — \emph{e} — the same vowel with no consonant under it
\end{quote}

A vowel that begins a word has nobody to ride on, so Devanagari gives it a letter of its own. Chapter 2 isolated \textbf{\mw{आ}} for \textbf{\mw{आभार}} and chapter 6 isolated \textbf{\mw{ई}} for the same reason. \textbf{\mw{ए}} is the third standing vowel this book has needed, and the first number is what needs it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Trace \textbf{\mw{ए}} three times, then write \textbf{\mw{े}} beside it and say which of the two needs a consonant. Finish with \textbf{\mw{क}}, which the next lesson puts to the right of \textbf{\mw{ए}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
This is the only sign the whole run of numbers adds.

Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ek]{Hear \emph{ek} — one}

\label{lesson:MW-C32-hear-ek}



\begin{quote}
Say final, say the final-price question, say bring it. Then write the letter from the last lesson.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{ek} — \textbf{one}
\end{quote}

One beat, and the vowel is the one whose letter the hand made a moment ago.

A seller has been naming amounts since chapter 27 and this book has been unable to hear a single one of them. That stops here. \emph{ek} is the first of twelve number words this slice teaches.

\emph{ek} also does work inside numbers far larger than itself. Marwari counts down to a round number as readily as up from one: the dictionary records \emph{ekuṇcālīs} for thirty-nine — one short of forty. Learn \emph{ek} and a piece of thirty-nine comes with it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ek]{\mw{एक} — one on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C32-ek}



\begin{quote}
Recall the three-word food payoff, write the word for final, and write \textbf{\mw{ए}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{ए}} + \textbf{\mw{क}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{एक}} — \emph{ek} — one
\end{quote}

Nothing joins and nothing changes shape. The standing vowel keeps its own head -line stroke, \textbf{\mw{क}} keeps its, and the two run together under one line.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\mw{एक}}, cover it, wait five seconds, write it. Check that the vowel letter, not the mark, is standing on the left.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[do]{Hear \emph{do} — two}

\label{lesson:MW-C32-hear-do-two}



\begin{quote}
Run the five-turn counter exchange in your head, say the final-price payoff, then say one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{do} — \textbf{two}
\end{quote}

Chapter 29 taught \emph{do} as an asking word: \textbf{hand it over}. This is the same sound and it will be the same two signs, with a second job.

Nothing marks which one is meant except where it stands. Before a thing, \emph{do} counts it. After a thing, in a request, \emph{do} asks for it. A learner who has met both hears the difference from the shape of the sentence, not from the word.

Rajasthani also prints \textbf{\mw{बे}} (\emph{be}) for two, alongside \emph{do}. Both are in use; this book counts with \emph{do} and names \emph{be} so a printed page holding it is not a surprise.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[do]{\mw{दो} — two on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C32-do-two}



\begin{quote}
Say flatbread, say the bring request, then say two.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{द}} + \textbf{\mw{ो}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{दो}} — \emph{do} — two
\end{quote}

The hand made this word in chapter 29. What is new is on the meaning side only: one written form, two jobs.

That is worth stating plainly, because it is why a page of Marwari can look as though it contains no numbers at all. A reader counting occurrences of \textbf{\mw{दो}} across this book finds seventeen of them, and every one is the asking word. The number had never been taught.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write \textbf{\mw{एक}} and \textbf{\mw{दो}} one under the other. Then write \textbf{\mw{पाणी} \mw{दो।}} underneath and mark which \textbf{\mw{दो}} counts.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tīn]{Hear \emph{tīn} — three}

\label{lesson:MW-C32-hear-teen}



\begin{quote}
Recall the five-word asking payoff, say water, then count as far as this book has taken you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{tīn} — \textbf{three}
\end{quote}

The vowel is long, and it is the same long vowel the ear learned in \emph{pāṇī} in chapter 4. Hold it. A short one turns the number into something else.

Count aloud: \emph{ek, do, tīn}. Three words in, and two of them arrived with no new sign for the hand at all.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tīn]{\mw{तीन} — three on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C32-teen}



\begin{quote}
Say the final-price question. Write flatbread and put a finger on its retroflex \textbf{\mw{ट}}. Then write one and two.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{त}} + \textbf{\mw{ी}} + \textbf{\mw{न}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{तीन}} — \emph{tīn} — three
\end{quote}

The \textbf{\mw{त}} here is the dental one, made with the tongue against the teeth — not the \textbf{\mw{ट}} of \textbf{\mw{रोटी}}, which is made further back. The two look different on the page and sound different in the mouth, and three uses the front one.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\mw{तीन}}, cover it, wait five seconds, write it. Then write \textbf{\mw{ट}} beside \textbf{\mw{त}} and say which one three needs.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chār]{Hear \emph{chār} — four}

\label{lesson:MW-C32-hear-chaar}



\begin{quote}
Say the hard wheat roll, say child, then count to three.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{chār} — \textbf{four}
\end{quote}

Put a hand in front of your mouth and say it. There is no puff of air on the opening consonant. That plain \emph{ch} is the one \textbf{\mw{बच्चा}} doubles.

Hold on to that, because the next chapter opens six with the same consonant carrying a puff. In Marwari, four and six begin a breath apart.

Count: \emph{ek, do, tīn, chār}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chār]{\mw{चार} — four on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C32-chaar}



\begin{quote}
Write the hard wheat roll, write the final-price question, then write three.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{च}} + \textbf{\mw{ा}} + \textbf{\mw{र}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{चार}} — \emph{chār} — four
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mw{र}} was the first sign this book ever asked the hand to make, in chapter 1, on the way to \textbf{\mw{राम}}. Thirty-one chapters later it closes the fourth number. Every sign in \textbf{\mw{चार}} is older than the market this number is for.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\mw{चार}}, cover it, wait five seconds, write it. Then write \textbf{\mw{एक}}, \textbf{\mw{दो}}, \textbf{\mw{तीन}}, \textbf{\mw{चार}} as a column and read the column back upward.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pāṅch]{Hear \emph{pāṅch} — five}

\label{lesson:MW-C32-hear-paanch}



\begin{quote}
Recall the five-word food payoff and the four-skill final-price payoff, answer yes respectfully, then say four.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{pāṅch} — \textbf{five}
\end{quote}

The vowel is nasal: the air goes out through the nose as well as the mouth. The ear met that in \textbf{\mw{हां} \mw{सा}} in chapter 3, and five is the first number to use it.

Four and five also close and open on the same consonant. \emph{chār} begins with the plain \emph{ch}; \emph{pāṅch} ends with it. Say them back to back and hear the sound move from the front of one word to the back of the other.

Count the whole set: \emph{ek, do, tīn, chār, pāṅch}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/soas/}{Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pāṅch]{\mw{पांच} — five on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C32-paanch}



\begin{quote}
Write the respectful yes, write four, say the bring-it word, and recall the five-word food payoff.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{प}} + \textbf{\mw{ा}} + \textbf{\mw{ं}} + \textbf{\mw{च}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{पांच}} — \emph{pāṅch} — five
\end{quote}

The dot above the head-line is the anusvara from chapter 3. It sits over \textbf{\mw{हां}} and it sits over \textbf{\mw{पां}} for the same reason: the vowel under it is nasal.

That is the whole cost of the first five numbers — one letter, \textbf{\mw{ए}}, and one mark the hand had already been making since the third chapter.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\mw{पांच}}, cover it, wait five seconds, write it. Check the dot. Then write \textbf{\mw{चार}} beneath it and mark the \textbf{\mw{च}} in both.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{The five, taken apart}

\label{lesson:MW-R32-count-recall}



\begin{quote}
Run the five-turn counter exchange, ask the price question aloud, write the bring-it word, then write \textbf{\mw{ए}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A run learned forwards is not yet a set of five words. Break it:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Hear one number on its own and say what it is. Then another, out of order.
  \item Count backwards from five.
  \item Read the five printed shuffled and say each.
  \item Write \textbf{\mw{तीन}}, \textbf{\mw{पांच}}, \textbf{\mw{एक}}, \textbf{\mw{चार}}, \textbf{\mw{दो}} from dictation in that order.
\end{enumerate}

Repair only the one that missed, and write it once more.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — counting to five}

\label{lesson:MW-C32-count-five}



\begin{quote}
Say the crumbled wheat sweet, say the bring request, then write the one letter this chapter added.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Four skills, scored separately.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Listening.} Hear five numbers named singly and out of order; write down which was said each time, in figures of your own language.
  \item \textbf{Speaking.} Count one to five, then five to one, without a model.
  \item \textbf{Reading.} Read the five printed in Devanagari, shuffled, and say each.
  \item \textbf{Writing.} Write all five from dictation, shuffled, with no model in view.
\end{enumerate}

Pass each one separately. A learner who can recite forwards and fails the shuffle has learned a rhyme, not five words.

This is the first amount the book can hear a seller name. What it still cannot do is hear anything above five, and a Rajasthani market prices very little at five or under.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Close the writing loop for \mw{ए}, \mw{क} and \mw{च}}

\label{lesson:MW-R32-script-close}



\begin{quote}
Recall the counting payoff and the five-word asking payoff, then write the crumbled wheat sweet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write three single signs from sound cues: \textbf{\mw{ए}}, \textbf{\mw{क}}, \textbf{\mw{च}}. Then write the mark \textbf{\mw{े}} beside \textbf{\mw{ए}} and say which of the two can stand at the front of a word.

Then write \textbf{\mw{एक}}, \textbf{\mw{दो}}, \textbf{\mw{तीन}}, \textbf{\mw{चार}}, \textbf{\mw{पांच}} from dictation, shuffled. Repair only the missed sign and rewrite its word once.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/rajasthani.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Rajasthani}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
